content: Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) is a member of the non-polio enterovirus group, which includes over 100 different viruses. These viruses are common, and most infections either cause no symptoms or result in mild symptoms. EV-D68 primarily causes respiratory illnesses, which can range from mild, such as symptoms resembling the common cold, to severe respiratory conditions. Children with asthma are at an increased risk of developing severe respiratory symptoms when infected with EV-D68. Unfortunately, there are currently no vaccines available to prevent EV-D68 infections. Symptoms of EV-D68 EV-D68 infections can present with a variety of symptoms, or in some cases, no symptoms at all. Mild symptoms include a runny nose, sneezing, coughing, and muscle or body aches. Severe symptoms may involve wheezing and difficulty breathing. In rare cases, EV-D68 can lead to a serious neurological condition called acute flaccid myelitis (AFM), which primarily affects children. AFM symptoms include sudden weakness in the arms or legs, pain in the neck, back, or limbs, difficulty swallowing, slurred speech, drooping eyelids, difficulty moving the eyes, and facial weakness. If you or your child experience any of these symptoms, especially after a respiratory illness, or if breathing becomes difficult, it is critical to seek medical attention immediately. Risk Factors Infants, children, and teenagers are more susceptible to EV-D68 infections because they have not yet developed immunity from previous exposures to enteroviruses. Adults can also become infected, but they are more likely to experience mild symptoms or remain asymptomatic. Children with asthma are particularly vulnerable to severe respiratory symptoms caused by EV-D68. Families with asthmatic children should follow CDC guidelines to manage asthma symptoms, especially during the enterovirus season, which typically occurs in the summer and fall in the United States. Transmission EV-D68 is a respiratory virus and is found in the respiratory secretions of infected individuals, such as saliva, nasal mucus, and sputum. The virus spreads through person-to-person contact, particularly when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or touches a surface that is subsequently touched by others. Prevention There are no vaccines to prevent EV-D68 infections. However, you can reduce the risk of infection by following general respiratory virus prevention measures. These include frequent handwashing, avoiding close contact with sick individuals, and disinfecting commonly touched surfaces. For individuals with asthma, it is essential to manage asthma symptoms effectively by adhering to an asthma action plan, taking prescribed medications, and ensuring access to reliever medications. Annual flu vaccination is also recommended to reduce the risk of complications from respiratory illnesses. Diagnosis Most healthcare providers cannot specifically test for EV-D68. Diagnosis requires specialized laboratory testing, such as PCR or molecular sequencing, which is performed by the CDC or certain state health departments. While many hospitals and doctors can test for general enterovirus infections, they may not be able to identify the specific type, such as EV-D68. Management and Treatment There is no specific antiviral treatment for EV-D68 infections. Management focuses on supportive care to alleviate symptoms. Individuals with severe respiratory illness may require hospitalization and intensive supportive therapy. For those with asthma, it is crucial to follow an updated asthma action plan, take prescribed medications, and seek medical attention if symptoms worsen or do not improve. Resources The CDC provides various resources to help individuals protect themselves and others from EV-D68. These include guidelines on handwashing, information about non-polio enteroviruses, and advice on managing asthma during enterovirus season.
